title: Germany wins Spruce Meadows Nations Cup as ‘team spirit’ proves indomitable
content:
Three weeks after winning the FEI Jumping World Championships in Aachen, Germany, the formidable German team topped the leaderboard again at the Spruce Meadows BMO Nations Cup in Calgary on Saturday to win the richest prize in team jumping.

Once again, Sophie Hinners proved to be the Germans’ crown jewel. Riding Iron Dames My Prins, she kept a clean sheet through both rounds, while teammates Daniel Deusser, Jörne Sprehe and Richard Vogel tipped a rail apiece.

It wasn’t always a given for the favorites, though.

Great Britain was dominant in Round 1. Both world No. 6 Ben Maher, riding Catelly, and Tim Gredley, riding Medoc de Toxandria, delivered fault-free rounds, allowing the team to drop Jessica Mendoza’s one-rail round with In The Air and keep the two time penalties collected by young gun Jack Whitaker and his horse, Jack JL. Their aggregate score put them two penalties ahead of Germany and six ahead of Ireland.

But a Nations Cup is never over until the last fence has been jumped — even when that last fence becomes arguably optional.

A spate of surprise fences — six after the first three riders — dropped the British team down to a provisional fourth place, putting the pressure on the Tokyo Olympic champion Maher.

Nothing could boost the British to the top of the podium at that stage in the competition, with Germany’s victory already secure before the final flight thanks to three sterling clears. But midway through that final flight, Belgium’s Emilie Conter opted to come forward. After three riders, her team sat on a score of 21. The British team, if it could drop the 12 penalties collected by Gredley and replace them with a characteristic clear from Maher, would move on to a total of 14.

Conter did exactly what an anchor should do. She jumped clear, delivering one of just 11 clears across the entire class. The effort forced Britain’s hand: If the British wanted to reach the podium, Maher had to jump, and he had to jump well. A clear would move them up to second, thanks to the withdrawal of Irish anchors Denis Lynch and Vistogrand. A one-rail, four-fault round would put the British into third ahead of Belgium for a respectable finish.

Then, seconds after the starter’s bell rang, Maher and Catelly fell.

Their turn to the first fence was perhaps a touch wider than their competitors; their canter, arguably, too freewheeling. But while a horse and rider of this calibre can reasonably expect to find their way to the landing side on pure physical ability, Catelly’s takeoff point was fractionally too far from the first fence. Though the 14-year-old gelding scrabbled in midair to try to regain his momentum, it was too late to save the effort. Catelly caught the back rail of the fence between his front legs, and horse and rider came crashing down.

It is a cruel irony that the first fence was a tribute to Belgium. Horse and rider — unharmed, but certainly winded — left the arena knowing that their fall had secured the podium place for the Belgians, just behind Ireland. Britain settled for fourth.

Germany’s Vogel was assured a team victory but opted to come forward anyway for his anchor round in pursuit of a clear-round bonus and valuable World Ranking points. His final-fence rail with the stallion Cloudio was Germany’s only second-round fault.

“We saw a really tough course today, but my horse is unbelievable,” Hinners said. “I’m the lucky one to be his rider — he’s so scopey, and I have the feeling that nothing is too big for him. He gave me so much.”

The Germans have, she said, “a great team spirit. We saw it at the World Championship in Aachen, and I think that’s given us the last percentages to have a good performance this week.”

Sunday’s Rolex Grand Prix, starting at 1 p.m. MDT, will be Spruce Meadows’ crescendo and one of the most hotly anticipated classes of the year. Vogel, mounted on the exceptional United Touch S, is aiming to become the second rider in history to win the Rolex Grand Slam of Showjumping — an elite title earned by winning three of four consecutive majors.

Their partnership warrants a place in the history books. The remarkable duo sent shockwaves across the world of showjumping just last month, however, when the stallion stopped at a fence in the individual final in Aachen. Perhaps, as in the world of theater, a bad dress rehearsal will pave the way to a brilliant opening night. Or maybe it is a loss of form at the moment it counts the most.
